liver.name: Liver
liver.description: The largest internal organ, in the upper right of the abdomen. It processes nutrients, makes bile, stores energy and breaks down toxins.
facts: Weighs about 1.5 kg in adults.
Makes bile, which helps digest fats.
Can regrow lost tissue.
Receives blood from both the hepatic artery and the portal vein.

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.description: A J-shaped muscular bag that stores food and starts digesting protein with acid and enzymes.
facts: Produces hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin.
Food enters from the oesophagus and leaves into the duodenum.
Its lining is protected from its own acid by a layer of mucus.

spleen.name: Spleen
spleen.description: An organ in the upper left of the abdomen that filters blood and helps fight infection.
facts: Removes old and damaged red blood cells.
Stores white blood cells and platelets.
People can live without a spleen, but they are more prone to some infections.

pancreas.name: Pancreas
pancreas.description: A gland behind the stomach that makes digestive enzymes and the hormones insulin and glucagon.
facts: Insulin and glucagon control blood sugar.
Its enzymes flow into the duodenum to digest food.
Diabetes is linked to problems with insulin.

gallbladder.name: Gallbladder
gallbladder.description: A small pear-shaped sac under the liver that stores and concentrates bile.
facts: Releases bile into the duodenum after a fatty meal.
Hard deposits called gallstones can form inside it.
It can be removed; bile then flows straight from the liver.

kidneys.name: Kidneys
kidneys.description: Two bean-shaped organs at the back of the abdomen that filter blood and make urine.
facts: Each kidney has about a million filtering units called nephrons.
Together they filter roughly 180 litres of blood plasma a day.
Also help control blood pressure and make hormones.
The right kidney usually sits a little lower than the left because of the liver.

adrenal_glands.name: Adrenal Glands
adrenal_glands.description: Small glands on top of each kidney that make hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol.
facts: Adrenaline prepares the body for 'fight or flight'.
Cortisol helps control metabolism and the stress response.
Also called suprarenal glands.

ureters.name: Ureters
ureters.description: Two thin tubes that carry urine from the kidneys down to the bladder.
facts: Each is about 25-30 cm long in adults.
Muscle waves (peristalsis) push urine along them.
Kidney stones can get stuck in them.

urinary_bladder.name: Urinary Bladder
urinary_bladder.description: A stretchy muscular bag in the pelvis that stores urine.
facts: Receives urine from the two ureters.
Its wall muscle is called the detrusor.
The urge to urinate usually starts when it holds a few hundred millilitres.

esophagus.name: Oesophagus
esophagus.description: The muscular tube that carries food from the throat to the stomach. Only its lower end is shown here.
facts: About 25 cm long in adults.
Moves food by waves of muscle contraction (peristalsis).
Passes through the diaphragm just before joining the stomach.

duodenum.name: Duodenum
duodenum.description: The first, C-shaped part of the small intestine, right after the stomach.
facts: Receives bile and pancreatic enzymes.
About 25 cm long.
Most digestion of food happens here and in the rest of the small intestine.

small_intestine.name: Small Intestine
small_intestine.description: The long, coiled tube where most food is digested and absorbed. Shown here: the jejunum and ileum.
facts: The whole small intestine is several metres long.
Its inner surface is covered in tiny finger-like villi that absorb nutrients.
The ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts.

large_intestine.name: Large Intestine
large_intestine.description: The final part of the gut, which absorbs water and forms stool. Shown here: the colon, appendix and rectum.
facts: About 1.5 m long, wider but shorter than the small intestine.
Home to trillions of gut bacteria.
The appendix is a small pouch attached to the start of the colon.
